title: Holoptelea integrifolia Bark and Leaf Extracts and the Bioactive Triterpenoids Friedelin and Lupeol Promote Keratinocyte Migration and Wound Repair via Hippo–MAPK Signaling
content: Cutaneous wound healing requires coordinated keratinocyte migration, proliferation, and epithelial remodeling. Natural products, particularly pentacyclic triterpenoids, have emerged as promising agents for tissue repair. Holoptelea integrifolia (Roxb.) Planch., a medicinal plant distributed across South and Southeast Asia and traditionally used for skin disorders and wounds, contains the bioactive triterpenoids friedelin and lupeol. However, the signaling mechanisms underlying the wound-repair effects of its extracts and bioactive compounds remain incompletely understood. This study investigated the wound-repair potential of H. integrifolia bark and leaf extracts and their major triterpenoids, friedelin and lupeol, using in vitro models and molecular analyses. Scratch assays in canine primary epidermal keratinocytes (CPEK) and human keratinocytes (HaCaT) showed that both extracts and triterpenoids significantly enhanced keratinocyte migration and accelerated wound closure in a concentration-dependent manner. Western blotting revealed increased Yes-associated protein (YAP) and transcriptional co-activator with PDZ-binding motif (TAZ) levels, accompanied by reduced mammalian sterile 20-like kinase 1 (MST1) and E-cadherin expression, supporting modulation of Hippo signaling toward a pro-migratory phenotype. Molecular docking predicted favorable interactions of friedelin and lupeol with MST1 and YAP. Collectively, these findings indicate that H. integrifolia extracts and their triterpenoids promote keratinocyte-mediated wound repair through coordinated modulation of Hippo and MAPK signaling, supporting friedelin and lupeol as natural candidates for cutaneous wound healing and skin regeneration.
